items.title: A Pandemic-Era Walk to a Mississauga Marsh Turned Into a Yearslong Conservation Mission for One Family
items.summary: According to The Pointer, Iyah, now a Mississauga tween, first noticed Osprey Marsh in the Lisgar neighbourhood back in fall 2020, when she was four years old and her family had just moved into the area during the pandemic. Iyah told the outlet the park's giant animal mural was impossible to miss from the car, and that it became one of the few places still open to her family while schools and activities shut down around them. She says she asked her mother, Jenna Evans, to take her to see it, and Evans agreed after weeks spent unpacking their new home. The Pointer reports the marsh sits a 10-minute walk from their house, near Ninth Line and Britannia Road West. Up close, mother and daughter found the animals painted on the mural were species that actually live in the marsh itself. That first visit marked the start of what has grown into Iyah's ongoing effort, years later, to protect the green space she found during one of the pandemic's quietest stretches.

items.title: INSAUGA Poll Finds Most Readers Unmoved by Mayoral Debates, But a Significant Minority Say Otherwise
items.summary: According to an INSAUGA Canada poll, most readers who responded say televised mayoral debates do not change how they vote, even as campaigns in Mississauga and Toronto head toward the Oct. 26 municipal election. The outlet put the question to readers after a string of high-profile face-offs, including matchups between Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish and former mayor Bonnie Crombie, who have sparred over affordability, housing, taxes and city finances. Toronto's race has seen its own debate stage showdowns, with Mayor Olivia Chow squaring off against Coun. Brad Bradford. INSAUGA reports that 865 participating readers said a debate could change who they vote for, a figure the outlet frames as representing more than four in 10 respondents. The poll suggests that while most voters walk into debate season with their minds already made up, a meaningful share remain open to persuasion before ballots are cast on election day.

items.title: Parrish vs. Crombie: As mayors past and present battle, will the drama drive voters to the polls?
items.summary: In Mississauga, incumbent Mayor Carolyn Parrish is facing former mayor Bonnie Crombie. With a crowded field and a high-profile showdown at the top of the ticket, the central question hanging over the campaign is whether the drama will actually get residents to the polls.

items.title: One Writer's Nervous Debut at a Mississauga Poetry Open Mic Opens a Window Into the City's Spoken Word Scene
items.summary: According to The Varsity, a University of Toronto student publication, reporter Nguyen Bao Han Tran set out to write about Mississauga's spoken word community but ended up performing in it herself, after her editor suggested she step up to the microphone rather than simply interview the poets she was covering. Tran writes that she became a Canadian citizen last year after immigrating from Vietnam. She says poetry long felt like a language within a language she could never quite master, even as she grew comfortable with English more broadly. Tran describes attending a Sauga Poetry open mic near her home in Mississauga one summer evening, reading a poem she had written and revised many times before taking the stage. She says she remembers the walk to the microphone more vividly than her poem's opening lines, with her heart pounding and sweat gathering along her back despite a cool room.

items.title: Crave Comedy Moves Queer Softball Team to Mississauga to Make Them 'A Little Less Cool'
items.summary: According to Insauga, Mississauga has landed an unexpected starring role in Slo Pitch, a new 10-episode Crave Original comedy that follows a struggling queer softball team more focused on beer, hookups and personal drama than actually winning games. The series follows the Public Lass Brovaries, an LGBTQ+ team competing in a fictional Mississauga slo-pitch league, and stars Jess Salgueiro as coach Joanne Pico alongside Schitt's Creek actor Emily Hampshire as her ex-girlfriend and rival, Leanne. The show premiered Sept. 25, released two more episodes on Oct. 2, and continues with new episodes every Friday. Co-creator and star Karen Knox told Toronto Today the production deliberately relocated the story from Toronto to Mississauga because the creators wanted the characters to feel a little less cool, while stressing the comment wasn't meant as a knock against the city. Knox said the move was meant to pull the characters away from what the creators saw as the intimidating, trendy queer scene of downtown Toronto and place them in a more suburban setting instead. The result follows a team of queer women and non-binary players navigating petty rivalries and relationship drama that make their beer-league season feel far more important than it really is.

items.title: Affordability Tops Mississauga Voter Concerns at 19 Percent, Ahead of Taxes and Housing, Poll Finds
items.summary: According to a Liaison Strategies poll from August 2026, affordability is the top concern among Mississauga voters heading into the municipal election, named by 19 per cent of respondents, ahead of taxes at 17 per cent and housing at 16 per cent. The paper reports that many residents are pushing candidates for property tax relief, even as economists warn that cutting revenue could strain city services and infrastructure. Mary Simpson, president of the Town of Port Credit Association, says property taxes are shaping how residents judge affordability in Mississauga. Simpson told the publication that the issue came up repeatedly at TOPCA's mid-year meeting in July, with multiple residents raising it as a top grievance. She said one man in his 60s told the group he is being priced out of his home and does not know how much longer he can stay in the city.

items.title: Burger King closes as Chick-fil-A plans move ahead in Mississauga
items.summary: A longtime Burger King that has been a familiar stop for west Mississauga residents has closed, and its departure appears to be clearing the way for a new Chick-fil-A at the site. The restaurant was located at 2460 Winston Churchill Boulevard at the southwest corner of Dundas Street West. While technically an Oakville address, the plaza is a popular shopping destination for residents in both communities, particularly people living in west Mississauga. The Burger King closed without warning recently, and the building now sits empty awaiting its future. And that future likely is a conversion into a Chick-fil-A restaurant. The Town of Oakville continues to list the location as an active site plan application by Chick-fil-A. The plans call for the existing single-storey fast-food restaurant to be demolished and replaced with a new single-storey restaurant with a double drive-through. The application has also progressed since the proposal was first reported by INSAUGA Canada earlier this year. The town’s development file shows multiple rounds of submissions, including revised plans submitted in February and another round of documents submitted in April.
